author: Horace
work: Epistulae, libri I-II, et Ars Poetica

pairs.source_text: Prima dicte mihi, summa dicende Camena, spectatum satis et donatum iam rude quaeris, Maecenas, iterum antiquo me includere ludo?
pairs.question: Quo dono gladiator Romanus emeritus missionem accipiebat, quo se donatum Horatius ad Maecenatem scribit?
pairs.question_en: By what gift did a Roman gladiator receive his discharge, the gift Horace says he has already been given, writing to Maecenas?
pairs.derivation: The rudis, the wooden foil handed to a gladiator on discharge, is the standing Roman image of retirement; Horace applies it to himself in the opening lines of the Epistulae. Anchored to Horace + Maecenas; one-word answer stated verbatim (donatum iam rude). Translatable and culturally salient: arena custom every Roman knew.

pairs.source_text: Non eadem est aetas, non mens. Veianius armis Herculis ad postem fixis latet abditus agro, ne populum extrema totiens exoret harena.
pairs.question: Cui deo Veianius gladiator arma sua fixit, cum harenam relinqueret?
pairs.question_en: To which god did the gladiator Veianius fix his arms when he left the arena?
pairs.derivation: Retiring gladiators dedicated their weapons at the doorpost of Hercules, patron of the arena. Anchored to the named gladiator Veianius; single-name answer stated verbatim (Herculis ad postem fixis). Closed-book cult-and-spectacle custom, not passage-dependent.

pairs.source_text: Non possis oculo quantum contendere Lynceus, non tamen idcirco contemnas lippus inungui;
pairs.question: Cuius herois oculorum acies apud Romanos in proverbio erat, quem Horatius lippo opponit?
pairs.question_en: Which hero's keenness of eye was proverbial among the Romans, whom Horace sets against the bleary-eyed man?
pairs.derivation: Lynceus the Argonaut is the canonical byword for sharp sight. Anchored by name; short answer supported verbatim. Shared mythological knowledge, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Est animus tibi, sunt mores, est lingua fidesque, sed quadringentis sex septem milia desunt: plebs eris.
pairs.question: Quantus census equiti Romano requirebatur, quo qui careret in plebe manebat, ut Horatius indicat?
pairs.question_en: What census rating was required of a Roman knight, without which a man stayed among the plebs, as Horace indicates?
pairs.derivation: The equestrian census of 400,000 sesterces, the threshold of the ordo equester. Anchored to the Roman census classes; a single number, stated verbatim (quadringentis... desunt: plebs eris). Institutional fact of Roman society, closed-book and translatable.

pairs.source_text: At pueri ludentes: 'Rex eris' aiunt, 'si recte facies': hic murus aeneus esto nil conscire sibi, nulla pallescere culpa.
pairs.question: Quid pueri Romani ludentes inter se canebant, ut Horatius refert?
pairs.question_en: What did Roman boys chant to one another at play, as Horace reports?
pairs.answer_en: 'You shall be king, if you do right.'
pairs.derivation: A children's game-formula of Roman childhood, quoted verbatim by Horace. Anchored to Roman boys at play + Horace; short quoted answer supported verbatim. Ambient custom, not doctrine.

pairs.source_text: olim quod uolpes aegroto cauta leoni respondit, referam: 'Quia me uestigia terrent, omnia te aduersum spectantia, nulla retrorsum.'
pairs.question: Qua de causa vulpes cauta in fabula ad leonem aegrotum intrare noluit, ut Horatius narrat?
pairs.answer: Quia omnia vestigia ad leonem spectabant, nulla retrorsum.
pairs.question_en: Why, in the fable Horace tells, did the wary fox refuse to go in to the sick lion?
pairs.answer_en: Because all the tracks pointed toward the lion, none back out.
pairs.derivation: The Aesopic fable of the sick lion and the fox, a shared story of the ancient world, quoted by Horace. Anchored to the named animals + the fable; answer stated verbatim. Short and checkable; not a moral.

pairs.source_text: Quo teneam uoltus mutantem Protea nodo?
pairs.question: Quem deum marinum, voltus mutantem, Horatius nullo nodo teneri posse queritur?
pairs.question_en: Which sea-god, changing his shape, does Horace complain cannot be held by any knot?
pairs.derivation: Proteus the shape-shifting sea-god, canonical myth. Anchored by name; one-word answer supported verbatim. Culturally salient shared story; translatable.

pairs.source_text: Troiani belli scriptorem, Maxime Lolli, dum tu declamas Romae, Praeneste relegi;
pairs.question: Quo in oppido Latii Horatius se Homerum relegisse ad Lollium scribit?
pairs.question_en: In which town of Latium does Horace write to Lollius that he re-read Homer?
pairs.derivation: Horace's re-reading of Homer at Praeneste, the frame of Epistle 1.2. Anchored to Horace + Lollius + the poet of the Trojan war; single place-name answer stated verbatim. Closed-book fact of literary biography and geography.

pairs.source_text: Quicquid delirant reges, plectuntur Achiui.
pairs.question: In cuius belli exemplo Horatius illud 'quidquid delirant reges, plectuntur Achivi' protulit?
pairs.question_en: Apropos of which war did Horace produce the tag 'whatever folly the kings commit, the Achaeans pay for it'?
pairs.derivation: One of Horace's most quoted tags, drawn in Epistle 1.2 from his reading of the Iliad (the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon, Paris' love, the walls of Troy). Anchored to the tag itself; the answer names the war the epistle is expounding. The Latin Library file prints 'Qucquid' for 'Quicquid', an evident typo of the conversion, corrected here.

pairs.source_text: Sirenum uoces et Circae pocula nosti;
pairs.question: Cuius mulieris pocula Ulixes, ut Horatius Lollium admonet, una cum Sirenum vocibus evasit?
pairs.question_en: Whose cups did Ulysses escape, along with the Sirens' voices, as Horace reminds Lollius?
pairs.derivation: The Odyssey's two great temptations named by Horace as common knowledge. Anchored to Ulysses + the Sirens; single-name answer supported verbatim. Shared myth, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet; sapere aude, incipe.
pairs.question: Cuius poetae Romani est illud 'dimidium facti qui coepit habet'?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet wrote 'he who has begun has half the deed done'?
pairs.derivation: A famous Horatian tag, whose checkable point is its authorship and place (Epistulae 1.2, to Lollius). Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer, supported verbatim by the source line.

pairs.source_text: Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet; sapere aude, incipe.
pairs.question: Quibus duobus verbis Horatius Lollium ad sapientiam capessendam hortatur, cum dimidium facti coepisse dicat?
pairs.question_en: With which two words does Horace urge Lollius to take up wisdom, having said that to begin is half the deed?
pairs.derivation: The tag sapere aude, later the motto of the Enlightenment, stands in Horace's Epistle 1.2 beside dimidium facti. Anchored to Horace + Lollius + the neighbouring tag; the two-word answer is verbatim in the source.

pairs.source_text: Ira furor breuis est; animum rege, qui nisi paret, imperat, hunc frenis, hunc tu compesce catena.
pairs.question: Quis poeta Romanus iram furorem brevem esse dixit?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet said that anger is a brief madness?
pairs.derivation: Ira furor brevis est, one of the best-known Latin sayings; the checkable fact is who wrote it (Horace, Epistulae 1.2). Anchored to the saying; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Iule Flore, quibus terrarum militet oris Claudius Augusti priuignus, scire laboro.
pairs.question: Quo gradu necessitudinis Tiberius Claudius Augusto iunctus erat, ut Horatius ad Iulium Florum scribit?
pairs.question_en: In what family relation did Tiberius Claudius stand to Augustus, as Horace writes to Julius Florus?
pairs.derivation: Tiberius as privignus of Augustus (son of Livia by her first husband). Anchored to both named men; short answer stated verbatim. Closed-book fact of the Augustan house.

pairs.source_text: Quid Titius, Romana breui uenturus in ora, Pindarici fontis qui non expalluit haustus, fastidire lacus et riuos ausus apertos?
pairs.question: Cuius poetae Graeci fontis haustus Titium non expalluisse Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: From which Greek poet's spring does Horace say Titius did not turn pale to drink?
pairs.derivation: Pindar as the perilous model for Latin lyric, a standing Augustan literary judgement. Anchored to Titius + the Pindaric spring; single-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid mihi Celsus agit? Monitus multumque monendus, priuatas ut quaeret opes et tangere uitet scripta, Palatinus quaecumque recepit Apollo,
pairs.question: In cuius dei templo Palatino scripta poetarum reposita erant, quae Horatius Celsum tangere vetat?
pairs.question_en: In which god's temple on the Palatine were the writings kept that Horace warns Celsus not to touch?
pairs.derivation: The library in the temple of Palatine Apollo, Augustus' great public collection. Anchored to Celsus + the Palatine temple; single-name answer stated verbatim. Institutional fact of Augustan Rome.

pairs.source_text: ne, si forte suas repetitum uenerit olim grex auium plumas, moueat cornicula risum furtiuis nudata coloribus.
pairs.question: Quae avis in fabula, plumis a ceteris avibus repetitis, furtivis coloribus nudata risum movet?
pairs.question_en: Which bird, in the fable, raises a laugh when it is stripped of its stolen colours as the other birds take back their feathers?
pairs.derivation: The Aesopic fable of the crow in borrowed plumage, cited by Horace as a warning against plagiarism. Anchored to the fable; one-word answer stated verbatim. Shared story, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Me pinguem et nitidum bene curata cute uises, cum ridere uoles, Epicuri de grege porcum.
pairs.question: Quo iocoso nomine Horatius se ipsum in epistula ad Albium appellat, sectam Epicuri significans?
pairs.question_en: By what joking name does Horace call himself in the letter to Albius, alluding to the school of Epicurus?
pairs.derivation: Horace's celebrated self-description, the standing joke about Epicureans. Anchored to Horace + Albius + Epicurus; short answer quoted verbatim from the source line.

pairs.source_text: Vina bibes iterum Tauro diffusa palustris inter Minturnas Sinuessanumque Petrinum.
pairs.question: Quo consule diffusum vinum Horatius Torquato apud se bibendum promittit?
pairs.question_en: Wine drawn off in whose consulship does Horace promise Torquatus at his table?
pairs.answer_en: In the second consulship of Taurus.
pairs.derivation: Roman wine was dated by the consuls of its vintage; Horace names Statilius Taurus' second consulship. Anchored to Horace + Torquatus + the named vintage; short answer stated verbatim. Food-and-drink culture, translatable.

pairs.source_text: cras nato Caesare festus dat ueniam somnumque dies; impune licebit aestiuam sermone benigno tendere noctem.
pairs.question: Cuius principis natalis dies apud Horatium festum diem facit, quo Torquatum ad cenam vocat?
pairs.question_en: Whose birthday makes the holiday on which Horace invites Torquatus to dinner?
pairs.derivation: The emperor's birthday as a public holiday, an Augustan institution of the calendar. Anchored to Horace's invitation + the named Caesar; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tu quotus esse uelis rescribe, et rebus omissis atria seruantem postico falle clientem.
pairs.question: Qua parte domus Horatius Torquatum clientem in atrio expectantem fallere iubet?
pairs.question_en: By what part of the house does Horace tell Torquatus to give the slip to the client waiting in his hall?
pairs.derivation: The client waiting in the atrium and the patron slipping out by the back door: the daily mechanics of Roman patronage. Anchored to Torquatus + his client; short answer stated verbatim (postico).

pairs.source_text: dum ficus prima calorque dissignatorem decorat lictoribus atris, dum pueris omnis pater et matercula pallet.
pairs.question: Quo colore vestitos lictores dissignatorem funerum comitari Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: Of what colour are the lictors that Horace says attend the funeral marshal?
pairs.derivation: The dissignator, master of ceremonies at Roman funerals, walked with black-clad lictors. Anchored to the named office; one-word answer stated verbatim. Funerary custom, the heart of criterion 8.

pairs.source_text: Non quo more piris uesci Calaber iubet hospes tu me fecisti locupletem.
pairs.question: Cuius regionis Italiae hospes apud Horatium hospitem piris vesci iubet, quae ipse porcis relicturus est?
pairs.question_en: A host of which region of Italy, in Horace, presses his guest to eat pears that he would otherwise leave to the pigs?
pairs.derivation: The 'Calabrian host' is Horace's proverbial figure of grudging, worthless generosity. Anchored to the named region + the pears; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: repserat in cumeram frumenti, pastaque rursus ire foras pleno tendebat corpore frustra; cui mustela procul: 'Si uis' ait 'effugere istinc,
pairs.question: Quod animal apud Horatium vulpeculae in cumeram frumenti inclusae suasit ut macra exiret qua macra subisset?
pairs.question_en: Which animal, in Horace, advised the little fox shut in the corn-bin to come out thin as it had gone in thin?
pairs.derivation: The fable of the fox in the corn-bin and the weasel's advice, a shared Aesopic story. Anchored to the fox + the corn-bin; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Haud male Telemachus, proles patientis Vlixei: 'Non est aptus equis Ithace locus, ut neque planis porrectus spatiis nec multae prodigus herbae;
pairs.question: Cur Telemachus apud Horatium equos ab Atrida sibi oblatos recusat?
pairs.answer: Quod Ithaca equis apta non est.
pairs.question_en: Why, in Horace, does Telemachus refuse the horses offered him by the son of Atreus?
pairs.answer_en: Because Ithaca is no place for horses.
pairs.derivation: The Odyssean scene of Telemachus at Sparta declining Menelaus' horses because rocky Ithaca cannot pasture them. Anchored to Telemachus + Ithaca; short answer stated verbatim. Shared story, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Strenuus et fortis causisque Philippus agendis clarus, ab officiis octauam circiter horam dum redit atque foro nimium distare Carinas iam grandis natu queritur,
pairs.question: Qua fere hora diei Philippus orator ab officiis domum redibat, ut Horatius narrat?
pairs.question_en: At about what hour of the day did the advocate Philippus return home from his business, as Horace tells it?
pairs.derivation: The Roman working day: business ends about the eighth hour. Anchored to the named Philippus; short numeric answer stated verbatim. Daily-life custom, translatable. (The Latin Library file prints 'circite' for 'circiter', an evident typo of the conversion, corrected here.)

pairs.source_text: It, redit et narrat Volteium nomine Menam, praeconem, tenui censu, sine crimine, notum
pairs.question: Quod artificium Volteio Menae erat, quem Philippus ad cenam vocavit?
pairs.question_en: What was the trade of Volteius Mena, whom Philippus invited to dinner?
pairs.derivation: The praeco, the auctioneer-crier of Roman public life, is the trade of Horace's Volteius Mena. Anchored to the named man; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: 'Sic ignouisse putato me tibi, si cenas hodie mecum.' 'Vt libet.' 'Ergo post nonam uenies; nunc i, rem strenuus auge.'
pairs.question: Post quam horam Philippus Volteium Menam ad cenam venire iussit?
pairs.question_en: After which hour did Philippus tell Volteius Mena to come to dinner?
pairs.derivation: The Roman dinner hour: cena begins after the ninth hour. Anchored to the two named men; short numeric answer stated verbatim. Ambient daily-life knowledge.

pairs.source_text: mane cliens et iam certus conuiua, iubetur rura suburbana indictis comes ire Latinis.
pairs.question: Quibus feriis indictis Philippus Volteium in rura suburbana comitem ire iussit?
pairs.question_en: At the proclamation of which festival did Philippus bid Volteius come with him to his country place near the city?
pairs.derivation: The Feriae Latinae, proclaimed each year by the consuls, emptied Rome for the Alban Mount rites. Anchored to the named men + the proclamation; short answer stated verbatim (indictis... Latinis). Calendar knowledge, criterion 8's home ground.

pairs.source_text: et sibi dum requiem, dum risus undique quaerit, dum septem donat sestertia, mutua septem promittit, persuadet uti mercetur agellum.
pairs.question: Quot sestertia Philippus Volteio Menae donavit, ut agellum emeret?
pairs.question_en: How many thousands of sesterces did Philippus give Volteius Mena to buy his little farm?
pairs.derivation: The sum of Horace's cautionary tale: seven sestertia given and seven lent. Anchored to the two named men + the farm; a single number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nil admirari prope res est una, Numici, solaque quae possit facere et seruare beatum.
pairs.question: Cuius poetae Romani praeceptum est illud 'nil admirari', ad Numicium scriptum?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet's precept is the famous 'nil admirari', written to Numicius?
pairs.derivation: The tag nil admirari, one of the most quoted phrases in Latin; the checkable point is its author and addressee (Horace, Epistulae 1.6, to Numicius). Anchored to the quoted words + the named addressee; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quicquid sub terra est, in apricum proferet aetas, defodiet condetque nitentia. Cum bene notum porticus Agrippae et uia te conspexerit Appi, ire tamen restat, Numa quo deuenit et Ancus.
pairs.question: Cuius viri porticum Horatius una cum via Appia inter celeberrima Romae loca nominat?
pairs.question_en: Whose portico does Horace name, along with the Appian Way, among the most frequented places of Rome?
pairs.derivation: The Porticus Agrippae and the Via Appia as the two places where a well-known man is seen: Augustan topography of Rome. Anchored to the named monuments; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: 'Qui possum tot?' ait; 'tamen et quaeram et quot habebo mittam'; post paulo scribit sibi milia quinque esse domi chlamydum; partem uel tolleret omnis.
pairs.question: Quot chlamydes Lucullus domi esse sibi rescripsit, cum centum scaenae praebendae rogatus esset?
pairs.question_en: How many cloaks did Lucullus write back that he had at home, when he had been asked for a hundred for the stage?
pairs.derivation: The anecdote of Lucullus' proverbial wealth (he is named two lines above: Chlamydes Lucullus, ut aiunt): asked for a hundred stage-cloaks, he finds five thousand at home. Anchored to Lucullus + the request; a single number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: mercemur seruum, qui dictet nomina, laeuum qui fodicet latus et cogat trans pondera dextram porrigere:
pairs.question: Quod ministerium praestabat servus quem Horatius emendum suadet ei qui gratiam apud populum captat?
pairs.question_en: What service was rendered by the slave Horace advises buying for a man who courts the people's favour?
pairs.answer_en: He prompted the names of those they met.
pairs.derivation: The nomenclator, the name-prompting slave of the Roman canvasser. Anchored to the candidate for popular favour; short answer stated verbatim (seruum, qui dictet nomina). Social custom of Roman public life, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Si, Mimnermus uti censet, sine amore iocisque nil est iucundum, uiuas in amore iocisque.
pairs.question: Cuius poetae Graeci sententia est nihil sine amore iocisque iucundum esse, ut Horatius refert?
pairs.question_en: Which Greek poet held, as Horace reports, that nothing is pleasant without love and jesting?
pairs.derivation: Mimnermus of Colophon, the elegist of love and pleasure, cited by name. Anchored to Horace + the doctrine attributed; one-name answer stated verbatim. Literary-cultural fact, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Naturam expelles furca, tamen usque recurret et mala perrumpet furtim fastidia uictrix.
pairs.question: Quis poeta Romanus scripsit naturam furca expulsam usque recursuram esse?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet wrote that nature, though driven out with a pitchfork, will always come running back?
pairs.derivation: Naturam expelles furca, one of the most quoted Latin proverbs; the checkable point is its author (Horace, Epistulae 1.10, to Aristius Fuscus). Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Haec tibi dictabam post fanum putre Vacunae, excepto quod non simul esses cetera laetus.
pairs.question: Cuius deae fanum apud agrum Sabinum Horatius nominat, unde epistulam ad Aristium Fuscum dictavit?
pairs.question_en: Whose shrine in the Sabine country does Horace name as the place from which he dictated the letter to Aristius Fuscus?
pairs.derivation: Vacuna, the old Sabine goddess whose crumbling shrine stood near Horace's farm. Anchored to Horace + the Sabine country; one-name answer stated verbatim. Local cult knowledge of the sort a Roman reader carried.

pairs.source_text: Quid tibi uisa Chios, Bullati, notaque Lesbos, quid concinna Samos, quid Croesi regia Sardis, Zmyrna quid et Colophon?
pairs.question: Cuius regis regiam urbem Horatius Sardis appellat?
pairs.question_en: Whose royal city does Horace call Sardis?
pairs.derivation: Sardis as the seat of Croesus, the byword for royal wealth. Anchored to the named city; one-name answer stated verbatim. Shared geographical-historical knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Scis Lebedus quid sit: Gabiis desertior atque Fidenis uicus; tamen illic uiuere uellem,
pairs.question: Quibus duobus Latii oppidis desertioribus Horatius Lebedum comparat?
pairs.question_en: With which two towns of Latium does Horace compare Lebedus, saying it is emptier than they?
pairs.derivation: Gabii and Fidenae as the proverbially deserted towns of Latium. Anchored to Lebedus + the comparison; two named places stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: caelum, non animum mutant, qui trans mare currunt.
pairs.question: Quis poeta Romanus scripsit eos qui trans mare currunt caelum, non animum mutare?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet wrote that those who race across the sea change their sky, not their mind?
pairs.derivation: A celebrated Horatian tag from the letter to Bullatius; the checkable point is its author and work. Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quod petis, hic est, est Vlubris, animus si te non deficit aequus.
pairs.question: Quod oppidum parvum Horatius nominat, ubi quod petimus inveniri possit, si animus aequus non desit?
pairs.question_en: Which small town does Horace name as a place where what we seek can be found, if a balanced mind does not fail us?
pairs.derivation: Ulubrae, the tiny Pomptine town, proverbial for obscurity, in one of Horace's most quoted closes. Anchored to the tag; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Fructibus Agrippae Siculis quos colligis, Icci, si recte frueris, non est ut copia maior ab Ioue donari possit tibi;
pairs.question: Cuius viri fructus Siculos Iccius colligebat, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: Whose Sicilian revenues was Iccius collecting, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: Iccius as steward of Agrippa's Sicilian estates. Anchored to the two named men; one-name answer stated verbatim. Fact of Augustan property and patronage.

pairs.source_text: Miramur, si Democriti pecus edit agellos cultaque, dum peregre est animus sine corpore uelox,
pairs.question: Cuius philosophi pecus agellos depastum esse fertur, dum animus eius peregre abest?
pairs.question_en: Whose fields, as the story goes, were eaten up by his own flocks while his mind was away abroad?
pairs.derivation: The anecdote of Democritus so absorbed in thought that his flocks ate his crops. Anchored to the named philosopher; one-name answer stated verbatim. Shared biographical lore.

pairs.source_text: Cantaber Agrippae, Claudi uirtute Neronis Armenius cecidit;
pairs.question: Cuius ducis virtute Cantaber cecidit, ut Horatius ad Iccium scribit?
pairs.question_en: By which commander's valour did the Cantabrian fall, as Horace writes to Iccius?
pairs.derivation: Agrippa's Cantabrian victory of 19 BC, reported by Horace as the news from Rome. Anchored to the Cantabri + Horace's letter; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cantaber Agrippae, Claudi uirtute Neronis Armenius cecidit;
pairs.question: Cuius virtute Armenius cecidit, ut Horatius ad Iccium scribit?
pairs.question_en: By whose valour did the Armenian fall, as Horace writes to Iccius?
pairs.derivation: Tiberius' Armenian settlement of 20 BC. Anchored to the Armenians + Horace's letter; name stated verbatim (Claudi uirtute Neronis).

pairs.source_text: ius imperiumque Prahates Caesaris accepit genibus minor;
pairs.question: Quis rex, genibus minor, ius imperiumque Caesaris accepit, ut Horatius ad Iccium scribit?
pairs.question_en: Which king, on bended knee, accepted Caesar's law and sway, as Horace writes to Iccius?
pairs.derivation: Phraates IV of Parthia submitting to Augustus, the diplomatic triumph of 20 BC. Anchored to Caesar + the submission; one-name answer stated verbatim in the Latin Library's spelling Prahates.

pairs.source_text: Vilice siluarum et mihi me reddentis agelli, quem tu fastidis habitatum quinque focis et quinque bonos solitum Variam dimittere patres,
pairs.question: Quot patres familias fundus Horati Sabinus Variam mittere solebat?
pairs.question_en: How many heads of household did Horace's Sabine estate regularly send down to Varia?
pairs.derivation: The size of Horace's Sabine farm: five hearths, five tenant fathers who sat in the council at Varia. Anchored to Horace's farm + Varia; a single number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam mihi Baias Musa superuacuas Antonius, et tamen illis me facit inuisum, gelida cum perluor unda per medium frigus;
pairs.question: Cuius medici auctoritate Horatius Baias supervacuas habuit, gelida potius unda perfusus?
pairs.question_en: On which physician's authority did Horace treat Baiae as superfluous, washing instead in cold water?
pairs.derivation: Antonius Musa, Augustus' doctor, whose cold-water regimen turned Roman fashion away from the warm springs of Baiae. Anchored to Horace + Baiae; name stated verbatim. Salient fact of Augustan medicine and fashion.

pairs.source_text: sulpura contemni uicus gemit, inuidus aegris qui caput et stomachum supponere fontibus audent Clusinis Gabiosque petunt et frigida rura.
pairs.question: Ad quorum locorum frigidos fontes aegri se conferebant, spretis Baiarum sulphuribus, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: To the cold springs of which places did the sick betake themselves, scorning the sulphur baths of Baiae, as Horace writes?
pairs.answer_en: To the springs of Clusium and to Gabii.
pairs.derivation: The cold-water cure that displaced Baiae: the springs of Clusium and Gabii. Anchored to Baiae + the invalids; two place-names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: aiebat, 'si qui comedunt bona, cum sit obeso nil melius turdo, nil uolua pulchrius ampla'.
pairs.question: Quas duas res in cena optimas esse Maenius apud Horatium dicebat?
pairs.question_en: Which two things did Maenius, in Horace, call the best at dinner?
pairs.answer_en: A fat thrush and a large sow's womb.
pairs.derivation: The two canonical delicacies of the Roman table, in the mouth of Horace's glutton Maenius (named at 1.15.26). Anchored to Maenius + the dinner; both items stated verbatim. Food culture, criterion 8's home ground.

pairs.source_text: 'Nec furtum feci nec fugi,' si mihi dicat seruos: 'Habes pretium, loris non ureris', aio. 'Non hominem occidi.' 'Non pasces in cruce coruos.'
pairs.question: Quod supplicium servum, qui hominem occidisset, apud Romanos manebat, ut Horatius indicat?
pairs.question_en: What punishment awaited a slave who had killed a man, as Horace indicates?
pairs.derivation: Crucifixion as the servile penalty (and the lash for theft). Anchored to the slave's plea; one-word answer stated verbatim (non pasces in cruce coruos). Legal and social fact, translatable.

pairs.source_text: labra mouet, metuens audiri: 'Pulchra Lauerna, da mihi fallere, da iusto sanctoque uideri, noctem peccatis et fraudibus obice nubem.'
pairs.question: Quam deam fur tacite precatur ut fallere et iustus videri liceat, ut Horatius describit?
pairs.question_en: To which goddess does the thief pray under his breath, that he may deceive and yet seem just, as Horace describes?
pairs.derivation: Laverna, the Roman goddess of thieves, with the whispered prayer that betrays the hypocrite. Anchored to the thief's prayer; one-name answer stated verbatim. Cult knowledge peculiar to Roman religion.

pairs.source_text: Vir bonus et sapiens audebit dicere: 'Pentheu, rector Thebarum, quid me perferre patique indignum coges?'
pairs.question: Cuius urbis rex Pentheus fuit, quem Horatius loquentem inducit?
pairs.question_en: Of which city was Pentheus king, whom Horace brings on speaking?
pairs.derivation: Pentheus, king of Thebes and antagonist of Bacchus, in Horace's dramatic dialogue. Anchored by name; one-place answer stated verbatim. Shared myth of the tragic stage.

pairs.source_text: Opinor, hoc sentit: 'Moriar'. Mors ultima linea rerum est.
pairs.question: Quis poeta Romanus mortem ultimam rerum lineam esse dixit?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet said that death is the final line of all things?
pairs.derivation: Mors ultima linea rerum est, a much-quoted tag closing Epistulae 1.16; its checkable point is authorship. Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Non cuiuis homini contingit adire Corinthum.
pairs.question: Ad quam urbem adire non cuivis homini contingere Horatius proverbio dicit?
pairs.question_en: To which city, in Horace's proverb, does it not fall to every man to go?
pairs.derivation: Horace's Latin rendering of the Greek proverb about Corinth's costly pleasures. Anchored to the proverb; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec semel inrisus triuiis attollere curat fracto crure planum, licet illi plurima manet lacrima, per sanctum iuratus dicat Osirim:
pairs.question: Per quem deum Aegyptium mendicus ille in triviis apud Horatium iurat?
pairs.question_en: By which Egyptian god does the beggar at the crossroads swear, in Horace?
pairs.derivation: The oath by Osiris in the mouth of a Roman street-beggar: the Egyptian cults in the city. Anchored to the crossroads beggar; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ambigitur quid enim? Castor sciat an Docilis plus, Brundisium Minuci melius uia ducat an Appi.
pairs.question: Quibus duabus viis Brundisium iri poterat, de quibus homines apud Horatium disputabant?
pairs.question_en: By which two roads could one travel to Brundisium, the point men disputed in Horace?
pairs.answer_en: By the Appian and the Minucian Way.
pairs.derivation: The two rival routes to Brundisium, a standard topic of Roman travellers' argument. Anchored to Brundisium; both road-names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Eutrapelus cuicumque nocere uolebat uestimenta dabat pretiosa; beatus enim iam cum pulchris tunicis sumet noua consilia et spes,
pairs.question: Quo dono Eutrapelus eos quibus nocere volebat corrumpebat?
pairs.question_en: By what gift did Eutrapelus ruin those he wished to harm?
pairs.derivation: The stratagem of Eutrapelus (P. Volumnius), a well-known Roman anecdote about the corrupting effect of finery. Anchored to the named man; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Zethi dissiluit, donec suspecta seuero conticuit lyra. Fraternis cessisse putatur moribus Amphion;
pairs.question: Uter geminorum fratrum, Amphion an Zethus, lyram deposuit ut fratris moribus cederet?
pairs.question_en: Which of the twin brothers, Amphion or Zethus, laid down his lyre to yield to his brother's ways?
pairs.derivation: The Theban twins Amphion the lyre-player and Zethus the herdsman, the canonical pair of contrasting brothers. Anchored to both names; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: sub duce qui templis Parthorum signa refigit nunc et, siquid abest, Italis adiudicat armis.
pairs.question: Quas res Romanas princeps ille, sub quo Lollius Cantabrica bella tulit, templis Parthorum refixit?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman things did the leader under whom Lollius served in the Cantabrian war take back from the temples of the Parthians?
pairs.derivation: The recovery of the standards lost at Carrhae, Augustus' celebrated Parthian settlement. Anchored to the Parthian temples + Lollius' commander; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: partitur lintres exercitus, Actia pugna te duce per pueros hostili more refertur; aduersarius est frater, lacus Hadria,
pairs.question: Cuius pugnae imaginem Lollius cum fratre per pueros in lacu paterno referebat?
pairs.question_en: Which battle did Lollius re-enact with his brother, using boys, on the lake of his father's estate?
pairs.derivation: The mock naval battle of Actium played on a country lake: Augustan spectacle turned into private game. Anchored to Lollius + his brother; the battle-name stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Consentire suis studiis qui crediderit te, fautor utroque tuum laudabit pollice ludum.
pairs.question: Quo gestu digitorum fautor apud Romanos ludum laudabat, ut Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: By what gesture of the fingers did a Roman supporter show his approval of a display, as Horace says?
pairs.derivation: The thumb as the Roman sign of favour in the arena and at games (utroque pollice). Anchored to the fautor + the ludus; short answer stated verbatim. Spectacle custom, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Me quotiens reficit gelidus Digentia riuus, quem Mandela bibit, rugosus frigore pagus
pairs.question: Quo nomine appellatur rivus gelidus qui Horatium in Sabinis reficit, quem Mandela bibit?
pairs.question_en: What is the name of the cold stream that refreshes Horace in the Sabine country, from which Mandela drinks?
pairs.derivation: The Digentia and the village Mandela, the topography of Horace's Sabine farm. Anchored to Mandela + the Sabine estate; one name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Prisco si credis, Maecenas docte, Cratino, nulla placere diu nec uiuere carmina possunt quae scribuntur aquae potoribus;
pairs.question: Cuius poetae Graeci veteris auctoritate Horatius negat carmina ab aquae potoribus scripta diu placere posse?
pairs.question_en: On which old Greek poet's authority does Horace deny that poems written by water-drinkers can please for long?
pairs.derivation: Cratinus, the Old Comedy poet, cited by Horace for the dictum that water-drinkers write nothing lasting. Anchored to Horace + Maecenas + the dictum; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: laudibus arguitur uini uinosus Homerus;
pairs.question: Quem poetam Horatius ex vini laudibus vinosum fuisse arguit?
pairs.question_en: Which poet does Horace convict of being a wine-lover on the evidence of his praises of wine?
pairs.derivation: Horace's joke on Homer, standard ancient literary lore. Anchored to the praises of wine; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ennius ipse pater numquam nisi potus ad arma prosiluit dicenda.
pairs.question: Quem poetam Latinum Horatius 'patrem' appellat, qui numquam nisi potus ad arma dicenda prosiluit?
pairs.question_en: Which Latin poet does Horace call 'father', the one who never leapt to sing of arms unless he had been drinking?
pairs.derivation: Ennius pater, the honorific of the founder of Latin epic, with the anecdote of his drinking. Anchored to the epithet + the claim; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Parios ego primus iambos ostendi Latio, numeros animosque secutus Archilochi, non res et agentia uerba Lycamben;
pairs.question: Cuius poetae Parii numeros Horatius se primum Latio ostendisse gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: Whose Parian measures does Horace boast that he first showed to Latium?
pairs.derivation: Horace's claim to have naturalised Archilochean iambus at Rome (the Epodes). Anchored to Latium + the Parian iambi; one-name answer stated verbatim. Literary history, translatable.

pairs.source_text: numeros animosque secutus Archilochi, non res et agentia uerba Lycamben;
pairs.question: Quem virum Archilochi res et agentia verba egerunt, quas Horatius se non secutum esse profitetur?
pairs.question_en: Which man was hounded by Archilochus' matter and driving words, which Horace declares he did not follow?
pairs.derivation: Lycambes, whom Archilochus' iambics destroyed, the standing example of the poet's deadly invective. Anchored to Archilochus; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: temperat Archilochi Musam pede mascula Sappho, temperat Alcaeus, sed rebus et ordine dispar,
pairs.question: Quos duos poetas Lesbios Horatius dicit Archilochi Musam eodem pede temperasse?
pairs.question_en: Which two poets of Lesbos does Horace say tempered Archilochus' Muse with the same foot?
pairs.derivation: The Lesbian pair, Sappho and Alcaeus, as heirs of Archilochus' metre: a fact about metrical descent that translates without residue. Anchored to Archilochus; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hunc ego, non alio dictum prius ore, Latinus uolgaui fidicen;
pairs.question: Quo se nomine Horatius appellat, qui carmen Lesbium primus Latio vulgavit?
pairs.question_en: By what name does Horace call himself, as the first to publish Lesbian song for Latium?
pairs.derivation: Horace's celebrated self-designation as Latinus fidicen, claiming the Aeolic lyric (Alcaeus, named three lines above) for Rome. Anchored to Horace + Lesbian song; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vortumnum Ianumque, liber, spectare uideris, scilicet ut prostes Sosiorum pumice mundus.
pairs.question: Quorum librariorum tabernam Horatius nominat, ubi liber eius Romae venalis prostet?
pairs.question_en: Whose bookshop does Horace name as the place where his book will stand for sale at Rome?
pairs.derivation: The brothers Sosii, Horace's booksellers (cf. Ars Poetica 345, hic meret aera liber Sosiis). Anchored to Horace's book + the Roman book-trade; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: me primis urbis belli placuisse domique, corporis exigui, praecanum, solibus aptum, irasci celerem, tamen ut placabilis essem.
pairs.question: Qualem se corpore et capillo Horatius in fine libri primi Epistularum describit?
pairs.question_en: How does Horace describe his own body and hair at the end of the first book of the Epistles?
pairs.answer_en: Small of body and grey before his time.
pairs.derivation: Horace's famous self-portrait, the chief ancient evidence for his appearance. Anchored to Horace + the close of Epistles I; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Forte meum siquis te percontabitur aeuum, me quater undenos sciat impleuisse Decembris collegam Lepidum quo duxit Lollius anno.
pairs.question: Quot annos natus Horatius librum primum Epistularum absolvit, ut ipse in ultima epistula significat?
pairs.question_en: How old was Horace when he finished the first book of the Epistles, as he indicates in the last letter?
pairs.derivation: Horace dates his own age at the close of Epistles I: quater undenos Decembris, forty-four Decembers. Anchored to Horace + the book's close; a single number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: me quater undenos sciat impleuisse Decembris collegam Lepidum quo duxit Lollius anno.
pairs.question: Quibus consulibus Horatius se quater undenos Decembris implevisse scribit?
pairs.question_en: In whose consulship does Horace write that he completed forty-four Decembers?
pairs.answer_en: In the consulship of Lollius and Lepidus.
pairs.derivation: Roman dating by the consuls of the year (21 BC, when Lollius took Lepidus as colleague). Anchored to Horace's own dating; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Romulus et Liber pater et cum Castore Pollux, post ingentia facta deorum in templa recepti, dum terras hominumque colunt genus, aspera bella componunt, agros adsignant, oppida condunt,
pairs.question: Quos heroas Horatius nominat, qui post ingentia facta in deorum templa recepti sint?
pairs.question_en: Which heroes does Horace name as having been received into the temples of the gods after their mighty deeds?
pairs.answer_en: Romulus, Father Liber, Castor and Pollux.
pairs.derivation: The canonical list of mortals raised to divinity, cited by Horace to Augustus. Anchored to Horace's letter to Augustus; the four names stated verbatim. Religious-cultural knowledge, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Diram qui contudit hydram notaque fatali portenta labore subegit, comperit inuidiam supremo fine domari.
pairs.question: Quod monstrum Hercules apud Horatium contudit, cum fatali labore portenta subigeret?
pairs.question_en: Which monster did Hercules crush, in Horace, as he subdued the famous prodigies by his fated labour?
pairs.derivation: Hercules and the Hydra, one of the canonical labours. Anchored to Hercules + the labours; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Praesenti tibi maturos largimur honores iurandasque tuom per numen ponimus aras, nil oriturum alias, nil ortum tale fatentes.
pairs.question: Quid Romani principi adhuc vivo posuerunt, per cuius numen iurarent, ut Horatius ad Augustum scribit?
pairs.question_en: What did the Romans set up to their still-living emperor, to swear by his divine power, as Horace writes to Augustus?
pairs.derivation: The living emperor's altars and the oath by his numen: the institution of the imperial cult. Anchored to Augustus + the honours; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: sic fautor ueterum ut tabulas peccare uetantis, quas bis quinque uiri sanxerunt, foedera regum uel Gabiis uel cum rigidis aequata Sabinis,
pairs.question: A quot viris tabulae legum Romanarum sanctae sunt, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: By how many men were the tablets of Roman law ratified, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: The Twelve Tables, drawn up by the decemviri: Horace's bis quinque uiri. Anchored to the tablets forbidding wrongdoing; a number answer stated verbatim. Foundational legal fact, translatable.

pairs.source_text: foedera regum uel Gabiis uel cum rigidis aequata Sabinis, pontificum libros, annosa uolumina uatum
pairs.question: Quorum duorum populorum foedera cum regibus Romanis icta Horatius inter vetusta Romanorum monumenta numerat?
pairs.question_en: With which two peoples does Horace count the old treaties of the kings among Rome's ancient documents?
pairs.derivation: The treaty with Gabii and the treaty with the Sabines, the oldest documents of Roman public law. Anchored to the kings' treaties; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ennius, et sapiens et fortis et alter Homerus, ut critici dicunt, leuiter curare uidetur quo promissa cadant et somnia Pythagorea.
pairs.question: Quo cognomine critici Ennium ornabant, ut Horatius refert?
pairs.question_en: By what title did the critics honour Ennius, as Horace reports?
pairs.derivation: Ennius as alter Homerus, the standard verdict of the Roman critics (and an allusion to his Pythagorean dream). Anchored to Ennius + the critics; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Naeuius in manibus non est et mentibus haeret paene recens? Adeo sanctum est uetus omne poema.
pairs.question: Cuius veteris poetae carmina Horatius adhuc in manibus esse et paene recentia mentibus haerere dicit?
pairs.question_en: Which old poet's works does Horace say are still in men's hands and stick in their minds as if new?
pairs.derivation: Naevius still read at Rome in Horace's day: a fact of the Roman literary canon. Anchored to the old poets; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ambigitur quotiens uter utro sit prior, aufert Paccuuius docti famam senis, Accius alti,
pairs.question: Quam famam Pacuvius poeta apud Horatium aufert?
pairs.question_en: What reputation does the poet Pacuvius carry off, in Horace?
pairs.answer_en: That of the learned old man.
pairs.derivation: The canonical Roman verdicts on the early tragedians: Pacuvius the learned, Accius the lofty. Anchored to Pacuvius; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: aufert Paccuuius docti famam senis, Accius alti,
pairs.question: Quo epitheto Accium tragicum Horatius ornat?
pairs.question_en: By what epithet does Horace honour the tragedian Accius?
pairs.derivation: Accius alti, the standing critical label for the greatest Roman tragedian. Anchored to Accius; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: dicitur Afrani toga conuenisse Menandro, Plautus ad exemplar Siculi properare Epicharmi,
pairs.question: Cui comico Graeco Afranii togam convenisse dicebatur?
pairs.question_en: To which Greek comic poet was Afranius' toga said to be suited?
pairs.derivation: The Roman critical commonplace pairing Afranius (writer of togatae) with Menander. Anchored to Afranius; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Plautus ad exemplar Siculi properare Epicharmi, uincere Caecilius grauitate, Terentius arte.
pairs.question: Ad cuius Siculi poetae exemplar Plautum properare Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: On which Sicilian poet's model does Horace say Plautus hurries along?
pairs.derivation: Plautus measured against Epicharmus of Sicily, a fixed judgement of Roman criticism. Anchored to Plautus; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: uincere Caecilius grauitate, Terentius arte.
pairs.question: Qua virtute Caecilium comicum vincere Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: In what quality does Horace say the comic poet Caecilius wins?
pairs.derivation: The canonical verdict on Caecilius Statius. Anchored to Caecilius; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: uincere Caecilius grauitate, Terentius arte.
pairs.question: Qua virtute Terentium vincere Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: In what quality does Horace say Terence wins?
pairs.derivation: The canonical verdict on Terence, paired against Caecilius. Anchored to Terence; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: habet hos numeratque poetas ad nostrum tempus Liui scriptoris ab aeuo.
pairs.question: A cuius scriptoris aetate Roma poetas suos numerare Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: From which writer's age does Horace say Rome counts her poets?
pairs.derivation: Livius Andronicus as the starting-point of Latin literature. Anchored to Rome's roll of poets; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Non equidem insector delendaue carmina Liui esse reor, memini quae plagosum mihi paruo Orbilium dictare;
pairs.question: Quo magistro Horatius puer carmina Livi Andronici ediscebat?
pairs.question_en: Under which schoolmaster did the boy Horace learn the poems of Livius Andronicus?
pairs.derivation: Orbilius, Horace's schoolmaster, and the use of Livius Andronicus as a school text. Anchored to Horace's boyhood + Livius; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: memini quae plagosum mihi paruo Orbilium dictare;
pairs.question: Quo cognomine Horatius Orbilium magistrum suum notavit?
pairs.question_en: By what epithet did Horace brand his schoolmaster Orbilius?
pairs.derivation: Plagosus Orbilius, the proverbial flogging schoolmaster of Roman education. Anchored to Orbilius; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Recte necne crocum floresque perambulet Attae fabula si dubitem, clament periisse pudorem cuncti paene patres,
pairs.question: Quibus rebus scaena Romana in ludis conspergebatur, per quas Attae fabula ambulabat?
pairs.question_en: With what was the Roman stage strewn at the games, through which Atta's play walked?
pairs.derivation: Saffron and flowers scattered on the Roman stage, a detail of theatrical luxury. Anchored to Atta's play + the stage; both items stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: cuncti paene patres, ea cum reprehendere coner quae grauis Aesopus, quae doctus Roscius egit,
pairs.question: Quos duos histriones nobilissimos Horatius nominat, quorum fabulas reprehendere paene nefas erat?
pairs.question_en: Which two most celebrated actors does Horace name, whose plays it was almost sacrilege to criticise?
pairs.derivation: Aesopus the tragic and Roscius the comic actor, the two great names of the Roman stage. Anchored to the Roman theatre; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Iam Saliare Numae carmen qui laudat, et illud quod mecum ignorat solus uolt scire uideri,
pairs.question: Cui regi carmen Saliare tribuebatur, quod Horatius laudari mirabatur?
pairs.question_en: To which king was the Salian hymn ascribed, which Horace marvels to hear praised?
pairs.derivation: The carmen Saliare, the archaic hymn of the Salian priests, ascribed to King Numa. Anchored to the hymn; one-name answer stated verbatim. Religious antiquity every Roman recognised.

pairs.source_text: Romae dulce diu fuit et sollemne reclusa mane domo uigilare, clienti promere iura, cautos nominibus rectis expendere nummos,
pairs.question: Quid Romae mane sollemne fuit erga clientem, cum domus reclusa esset?
pairs.question_en: What was the solemn morning practice at Rome toward a client, once the house was thrown open?
pairs.derivation: The morning salutatio: the patron opens his house at dawn and expounds the law to his clients. Anchored to Rome + the client; short answer stated verbatim. Central custom of Roman social life.

pairs.source_text: Mutauit mentem populus leuis et calet uno scribendi studio; pueri patresque seueri fronde comas uincti cenant et carmina dictant.
pairs.question: Qua re Romani inter cenam comas vinciebant, ut Horatius de scribendi studio queritur?
pairs.question_en: With what did Romans bind their hair at dinner, as Horace complains of the craze for writing?
pairs.derivation: Garlands of foliage worn by diners: the standing dress of the Roman dinner-party. Anchored to the cena; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: cum sociis operum pueris et coniuge fida Tellurem porco, Siluanum lacte piabant, floribus et uino Genium memorem breuis aeui.
pairs.question: Qua hostia agricolae prisci Tellurem piabant, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: With what victim did the old farmers propitiate Earth (Tellus), as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: The rustic harvest rite: the pig for Tellus. Anchored to the named deity + the old farmers; one-word answer stated verbatim. Sacrificial practice, the core of criterion 8.

pairs.source_text: Tellurem porco, Siluanum lacte piabant, floribus et uino Genium memorem breuis aeui.
pairs.question: Qua re agricolae prisci Silvanum piabant, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: With what did the old farmers propitiate Silvanus, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: The milk offering to Silvanus, god of the woodland boundary. Anchored to the named deity; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tellurem porco, Siluanum lacte piabant, floribus et uino Genium memorem breuis aeui.
pairs.question: Quibus duabus rebus agricolae prisci Genium placabant, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: With which two things did the old farmers appease the Genius, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: The offering to the Genius at the harvest festival: flowers and wine, not blood. Anchored to the Genius; both items stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Fescennina per hunc inuenta licentia morem uersibus alternis opprobria rustica fudit,
pairs.question: Quo modo Fescennina licentia opprobria rustica inter agricolas fundebat?
pairs.question_en: In what form did Fescennine licence pour out its rustic abuse among the farmers?
pairs.derivation: The Fescennine verses, exchanged in alternate lines at country festivals: the origin Horace gives for Roman abusive verse. Anchored to the named licence; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quin etiam lex poenaque lata, malo quae nollet carmine quemquam describi; uertere modum, formidine fustis ad bene dicendum delectandumque redacti.
pairs.question: Quid lex Romana de malo carmine sanxit, ut Horatius narrat?
pairs.question_en: What did the Roman law lay down about the malum carmen, as Horace tells it?
pairs.answer_en: That no one should be lampooned in an evil song.
pairs.derivation: The clause of the Twelve Tables penalising defamatory verse, which Horace makes the check on Fescennine abuse. Anchored to the law + the malum carmen; short answer stated verbatim. Legal fact, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Graecia capta ferum uictorem cepit et artes intulit agresti Latio;
pairs.question: Cuius poetae Romani est illud 'Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit', de artibus in Latium invectis?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet wrote 'captive Greece took her fierce conqueror captive', of the arts brought into Latium?
pairs.derivation: The single most quoted line on Rome's conquest by Greek culture; its checkable point is authorship and subject (Horace, Epistulae 2.1, to Augustus). Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: sic horridus ille defluxit numerus Saturnius, et graue uirus munditiae pepulere;
pairs.question: Quo nomine appellatur ille horridus numerus, qui Graecis artibus in Latium invectis defluxit?
pairs.question_en: What was the name of the rough measure that ebbed away when Greek art came into Latium?
pairs.derivation: The Saturnian, the native Italian verse displaced by Greek metres: a fact about metre that names the metre and therefore translates without residue. Anchored to the arrival of Greek art; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Serus enim Graecis admouit acumina chartis et post Punica bella quietus quaerere coepit, quid Sophocles et Thespis et Aeschylos utile ferrent.
pairs.question: Post quae bella Romanus Graecis chartis acumina admovere coepit, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: After which wars did the Roman begin to apply his wits to Greek writings, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: Horace's dating of Rome's turn to Greek literature. Anchored to Rome + the Greek books; short answer stated verbatim. Literary-historical fact, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Aspice, Plautus quo pacto partis tutetur amantis ephebi, ut patris attenti, lenonis ut insidiosi,
pairs.question: Cuius poetae Romani personas — amantis ephebi, patris attenti, lenonis insidiosi — Horatius commemorat?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet's stock roles - the young lover, the tight-fisted father, the scheming pimp - does Horace recall?
pairs.derivation: The stock characters of Roman comedy as Horace lists them for Plautus. Anchored to the named roles; one-name answer stated verbatim. Theatrical convention, translatable.

pairs.source_text: quantus sit Dossennus edacibus in parasitis, quam non adstricto percurrat pulpita socco;
pairs.question: Quo calceamento comoediae proprio Plautum pulpita percurrere Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: In what footwear proper to comedy does Horace say Plautus races over the boards?
pairs.derivation: The soccus, the low slipper of comedy as against the tragic cothurnus. Anchored to Plautus + the stage; one-word answer stated verbatim. Stage convention, translatable.

pairs.source_text: indocti stolidique et depugnare parati si discordet eques, media inter carmina poscunt aut ursum aut pugiles; his nam plebecula gaudet.
pairs.question: Quid plebecula media inter carmina in theatro poscere solebat, ut Horatius ad Augustum queritur?
pairs.question_en: What did the crowd call for in the middle of a play, as Horace complains to Augustus?
pairs.derivation: The Roman audience interrupting a play to demand a bear-baiting or boxers. Anchored to the theatre crowd; short answer stated verbatim. Spectacle custom, the essence of criterion 8.

pairs.source_text: Quattuor aut pluris aulaea premuntur in horas dum fugiunt equitum turmae peditumque cateruae;
pairs.question: Quot fere horas aulaea premuntur, dum equitum turmae peditumque catervae in scaena fugiunt?
pairs.question_en: For about how many hours is the curtain kept down while squadrons of horse and companies of foot flee across the stage?
pairs.derivation: The Roman stage-curtain (lowered, not raised) and the length of the spectacle-parades. Anchored to the theatre; a number answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Si foret in terris, rideret Democritus, seu diuersum confusa genus panthera camelo siue elephans albus uolgi conuerteret ora;
pairs.question: Quis philosophus, si in terris esset, spectacula Romana risurus erat, ut Horatius fingit?
pairs.question_en: Which philosopher, were he on earth, would laugh at the Roman shows, as Horace imagines?
pairs.derivation: Democritus the laughing philosopher, set by Horace in the Roman theatre. Anchored to the shows; one-name answer stated verbatim. Shared cultural type.

pairs.source_text: seu diuersum confusa genus panthera camelo siue elephans albus uolgi conuerteret ora;
pairs.question: Quae duo animalia peregrina Horatius nominat, quae vulgi ora in ludis converterent?
pairs.answer: Pantheram camelo confusam et elephantum album.
pairs.question_en: Which two foreign animals does Horace name as turning the crowd's faces at the games?
pairs.answer_en: A panther crossed with a camel (the giraffe) and a white elephant.
pairs.derivation: The exotic beasts displayed at Roman shows: the camelopard and the white elephant. Anchored to the games; both stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dixit adhuc aliquid? Nil sane. Quid placet ergo? Lana Tarentino uiolas imitata ueneno.
pairs.question: Cuius urbis colore lana violas imitata tinguebatur, quae in scaena spectatoribus placebat?
pairs.question_en: With which city's dye was the wool coloured that imitated violets and delighted the audience on stage?
pairs.derivation: Tarentine purple, the famous dye of the Greek south of Italy, on stage costume. Anchored to the theatre + the wool; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Gratus Alexandro regi Magno fuit ille Choerilos, incultis qui uersibus et male natis rettulit acceptos, regale nomisma, Philippos.
pairs.question: Cui regi Choerilus poeta gratus fuit?
pairs.question_en: To which king was the poet Choerilus welcome?
pairs.derivation: Choerilus, Alexander's bad court poet, the standing example of a king's misplaced patronage. Anchored to Choerilus; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: incultis qui uersibus et male natis rettulit acceptos, regale nomisma, Philippos.
pairs.question: Quo nomismate regio Choerilus poeta pro versibus suis donabatur?
pairs.question_en: In what royal coin was the poet Choerilus paid for his verses?
pairs.derivation: The Philippus, the gold coin of the Macedonian kings, named for Philip. Anchored to Choerilus + the royal coinage; one-word answer stated verbatim. Money knowledge, translatable.

pairs.source_text: edicto uetuit nequis se praeter Apellen pingeret aut alius Lysippo duceret aera fortis Alexandri uoltum simulantia.
pairs.question: Quis pictor solus, Alexandri edicto, regem pingere permissus est?
pairs.question_en: Which painter alone was allowed by Alexander's edict to paint the king?
pairs.derivation: Alexander's edict reserving his portrait to Apelles: a famous fact of ancient art history. Anchored to Alexander's edict; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: aut alius Lysippo duceret aera fortis Alexandri uoltum simulantia.
pairs.question: Cui soli artifici licuit Alexandri voltum ex aere ducere?
pairs.question_en: Which craftsman alone was permitted to cast Alexander's likeness in bronze?
pairs.derivation: Lysippus as Alexander's only authorised sculptor in bronze, the companion fact to Apelles. Anchored to Alexander's edict; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: At neque dedecorant tua de se iudicia atque munera, quae multa dantis cum laude tulerunt dilecti tibi Vergilius Variusque poetae,
pairs.question: Quos duos poetas Horatius Augusto dilectos nominat, qui munera eius cum laude acceperunt?
pairs.question_en: Which two poets does Horace name as dear to Augustus, who received his gifts to the giver's credit?
pairs.derivation: Virgil and Varius as the poets of Augustus' patronage. Anchored to Augustus + his gifts; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: claustraque custodem pacis cohibentia Ianum et formidatam Parthis te principe Romam,
pairs.question: Cuius dei claustra, pace parta, clausa cohibent, ut Horatius ad Augustum canit?
pairs.question_en: Which god do the bars shut in when peace has been won, as Horace sings to Augustus?
pairs.derivation: The closing of the gates of Janus in time of peace, one of the signal Augustan acts. Anchored to Augustus' peace; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: deferar in uicum uendentem tus et odores et piper et quicquid chartis amicitur ineptis.
pairs.question: Ad quas merces involvendas chartae ineptae adhibebantur, ut Horatius iocatur?
pairs.answer: Ad tus et odores et piper.
pairs.question_en: For wrapping what wares was useless writing-paper used, as Horace jokes?
pairs.derivation: The Roman joke that failed books end as wrapping in the spice-sellers' street. Anchored to the book trade; the three wares stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: 'Hic et candidus et talos a uertice pulcher ad imos fiet eritque tuus nummorum milibus octo,
pairs.question: Quanti pretii puer ille venalis in epistula Horati ad Florum offertur?
pairs.question_en: At what price is the slave boy offered for sale in Horace's letter to Florus?
pairs.derivation: The going price of a handsome, Greek-schooled slave boy: eight thousand sesterces. Anchored to Horace's letter + the sale; a single figure stated verbatim. Fact of the Roman slave market, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Luculli miles collecta uiatica multis aerumnis, lassus dum noctu stertit, ad assem perdiderat;
pairs.question: Cuius ducis miles, viatico noctu amisso, praesidium regale loco deiecit, ut Horatius narrat?
pairs.question_en: Whose soldier, after losing his savings in the night, dislodged a royal garrison, as Horace tells it?
pairs.derivation: The tale of Lucullus' soldier, the exemplum of poverty making men brave. Anchored to the named general; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Clarus ob id factum donis ornatur honestis, accipit et bis dena super sestertia nummum.
pairs.question: Quantam pecuniam miles ille Luculli pro forti facto accepit?
pairs.question_en: How much money did that soldier of Lucullus receive for his brave deed?
pairs.derivation: The soldier's reward, twice ten thousand sesterces over and above the decorations. Anchored to the soldier + Lucullus; a figure stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Post haec ille catus, quantumuis rusticus: 'Ibit, ibit eo, quo uis, qui zonam perdidit' inquit.
pairs.question: Quid miles ille praetori respondit, cum ad castellum expugnandum hortaretur?
pairs.answer: 'Ibit eo quo vis, qui zonam perdidit.'
pairs.question_en: What did the soldier answer the praetor who urged him to storm a fort?
pairs.answer_en: 'He will go where you like - the man who has lost his money-belt.'
pairs.derivation: The soldier's proverbial retort, the point of Horace's exemplum. Anchored to the soldier + the praetor; the saying quoted verbatim from the source.

pairs.source_text: Romae nutriri mihi contigit atque doceri iratus Grais quantum nocuisset Achilles. Adiecere bonae paulo plus artis Athenae,
pairs.question: In qua urbe Graeca Horatius studia sua auxit, Romae iam eruditus?
pairs.question_en: In which Greek city did Horace add to his studies, after his schooling at Rome?
pairs.derivation: Horace's education: Rome first, then Athens. Anchored to Horace + Rome; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Romae nutriri mihi contigit atque doceri iratus Grais quantum nocuisset Achilles.
pairs.question: Cuius herois ira Romae in ludo Horatio puero praelegebatur?
pairs.question_en: Which hero's wrath was read to the boy Horace in the schoolroom at Rome?
pairs.derivation: Homer's Iliad as the Roman schoolbook, described by its opening theme. Anchored to Roman schooling + Horace; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: scilicet ut uellem curuo dinoscere rectum atque inter siluas Academi quaerere uerum.
pairs.question: In quibus silvis Athenis Horatius verum quaerebat?
pairs.question_en: In which groves at Athens did Horace seek the truth?
pairs.derivation: The Academy, Plato's grove at Athens, where Horace studied. Anchored to Athens + Horace; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ciuilisque rudem belli tulit aestus in arma Caesaris Augusti non responsura lacertis. Vnde simul primum me dimisere Philippi,
pairs.question: In quo proelio Horatius arma contra Caesarem Augustum tulisse et inde dimissus esse se fatetur?
pairs.question_en: In which battle does Horace admit he bore arms against Caesar Augustus and was thence discharged?
pairs.derivation: Horace's own testimony to his service on the losing side at Philippi. Anchored to Horace + Augustus; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: decisis humilem pinnis inopemque paterni et laris et fundi paupertas impulit audax ut uersus facerem;
pairs.question: Quae res Horatium, patrio lare et fundo amisso, ad versus faciendos impulit?
pairs.question_en: What drove Horace, stripped of his father's house and land, to make verses?
pairs.derivation: Horace's account of why he began to write: the confiscation after Philippi and consequent poverty. Anchored to Horace + the lost estate; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Frater erat Romae consulti rhetor, ut alter alterius sermone meros audiret honores, Gracchus ut hic illi, foret huic ut Mucius ille.
pairs.question: Quos duos viros Horatius exempla ponit, alterum eloquentiae, alterum iuris peritiae?
pairs.question_en: Which two men does Horace set up as models, one of eloquence, the other of legal learning?
pairs.derivation: Gracchus as the type of the orator, Mucius Scaevola as the type of the jurist: the Roman shorthand for the two professions. Anchored to the rhetor and the iuris consultus; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Caedimur et totidem plagis consumimus hostem, lento Samnites ad lumina prima duello.
pairs.question: Quod genus gladiatorum Horatius nominat, quorum lentum duellum ad lumina prima ducitur?
pairs.question_en: Which class of gladiators does Horace name, whose slow duel drags on till the lamps are lit?
pairs.derivation: The Samnis, one of the named gladiatorial types of the Roman arena. Anchored to the duel + the lamps; one-word answer stated verbatim. Spectacle knowledge, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Fuit haud ignobilis Argis, qui se credebat miros audire tragoedos in uacuo laetus sessor plausorque theatro,
pairs.question: Quid ille Argivus insanus in vacuo theatro sedens se audire credebat?
pairs.question_en: What did that madman of Argos, sitting in an empty theatre, believe he was hearing?
pairs.derivation: The famous Argive who applauded plays in an empty theatre, Horace's parable of happy delusion. Anchored to Argos + the empty theatre; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hic ubi cognatorum opibus curisque refectus expulit elleboro morbum bilemque meraco et redit ad sese:
pairs.question: Quo medicamento ille Argivus insanus morbum bilemque expulit?
pairs.question_en: With what drug did that Argive madman drive out his disease and bile?
pairs.derivation: Hellebore as the ancient cure for madness (whence the proverbial Anticyra). Anchored to the Argive madman; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Si proprium est quod quis libra mercatus et aere est, quaedam, si credis consultis, mancipat usus,
pairs.question: Quibus duabus rebus adhibitis res apud Romanos mancipio emebatur, ut Horatius ad Florum scribit?
pairs.question_en: By the use of which two things was property bought by mancipation among the Romans, as Horace writes to Florus?
pairs.derivation: Mancipatio per aes et libram, the formal Roman conveyance. Anchored to Roman ownership + the jurists; both items stated verbatim. Legal institution, translatable.

pairs.source_text: quaedam, si credis consultis, mancipat usus, qui te pascit ager, tuus est,
pairs.question: Quo modo, si iuris consultis credis, quaedam res sine mancipatione fiunt propriae, ut Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: By what means, if you believe the jurists, do certain things become one's own without formal conveyance, as Horace says?
pairs.derivation: Usucapio, acquisition of ownership by long use, cited by Horace from the jurists. Anchored to the consulti; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: sed uocat usque suum, qua populus adsita certis limitibus uicina refugit iurgia;
pairs.question: Quae arbor certis limitibus adserebatur, ut vicina iurgia refugerentur, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: Which tree was planted along fixed boundaries to keep off quarrels with the neighbours, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: Poplars planted as boundary markers on Italian farms. Anchored to the field boundaries; one-word answer stated verbatim. Agrarian custom, translatable.

pairs.source_text: scit Genius, natale comes qui temperat astrum, naturae deus humanae, mortalis in unum quodque caput, uoltu mutabilis, albus et ater.
pairs.question: Qui deus, ut Horatius scribit, natale cuiusque astrum comes temperat?
pairs.question_en: Which god, as Horace writes, attends and governs each man's birth-star?
pairs.derivation: The Genius, the god born with each man and dying with him: the definition Horace gives. Anchored to the birth-star; one-word answer stated verbatim. Roman religion proper.

pairs.source_text: ac potius, puer ut festis Quinquatribus olim, exiguo gratoque fruaris tempore raptim.
pairs.question: Quibus feriis pueri Romani a ludo litterario vacabant, quas Horatius exempli causa ponit?
pairs.question_en: At which festival did Roman schoolboys get their holiday, the one Horace cites as an example?
pairs.derivation: The Quinquatrus of March, Minerva's festival and the schoolboys' holiday. Anchored to Roman boys + the festival; one-word answer stated verbatim. Calendar knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Somnia, terrores magicos, miracula, sagas, nocturnos lemures portentaque Thessala rides?
pairs.question: Cuius regionis portenta Horatius inter magicos terrores numerat?
pairs.question_en: Which region's portents does Horace count among the terrors of magic?
pairs.derivation: Thessaly as the proverbial home of witchcraft in the Roman imagination. Anchored to the list of magical terrors; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Somnia, terrores magicos, miracula, sagas, nocturnos lemures portentaque Thessala rides?
pairs.question: Quo nomine Romani nocturnas umbras mortuorum appellabant, quas Horatius inter terrores numerat?
pairs.question_en: By what name did the Romans call the night-walking ghosts of the dead, which Horace lists among terrors?
pairs.derivation: The lemures, the Roman night-ghosts placated at the Lemuria. Anchored to the list of night terrors; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Lusisti satis, edisti satis atque bibisti; tempus abire tibi est,
pairs.question: Quis poeta Romanus scripsit 'lusisti satis, edisti satis atque bibisti; tempus abire tibi est'?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman poet wrote 'you have played enough, eaten and drunk enough; it is time for you to go'?
pairs.derivation: The closing tag of the second book of Epistles, much quoted; its checkable point is authorship and place. Anchored to the quoted words; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Humano capiti ceruicem pictor equinam iungere si uelit et uarias inducere plumas undique collatis membris, ut turpiter atrum desinat in piscem mulier formosa superne,
pairs.question: In quam bestiam mulier superne formosa desinit in illa pictura, qua Horatius Artem Poeticam incipit?
pairs.question_en: Into what creature does the woman, lovely above, end in the picture with which Horace opens the Ars Poetica?
pairs.derivation: The monstrous composite picture that opens the Ars Poetica, one of the best-known images in Latin criticism. Anchored to the opening of the work; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: "Pictoribus atque poetis quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas."
pairs.question: Quibus duobus artificibus par audendi potestas semper fuisse dicitur, ut in Arte Poetica legitur?
pairs.question_en: Which two kinds of craftsman have always had, as the Ars Poetica quotes it, an equal licence to dare anything?
pairs.derivation: The famous claim quoted (and qualified) by Horace, endlessly cited in later criticism. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; both named verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Inceptis grauibus plerumque et magna professis purpureus, late qui splendeat, unus et alter adsuitur pannus,
pairs.question: Quo colore est pannus ille, qui gravibus inceptis adsui solet, ut Horatius in Arte Poetica dicit?
pairs.question_en: What colour is the patch that is commonly sewn onto grave beginnings, as Horace says in the Ars Poetica?
pairs.derivation: The purpureus pannus, origin of the phrase 'purple patch'. Anchored to Horace's criticism of irrelevant ornament; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Amphora coepit institui; currente rota cur urceus exit?
pairs.question: Quid ex rota currente exit, cum amphora institui coepta sit, ut Horatius quaerit?
pairs.question_en: What comes off the spinning wheel, when a wine-jar was begun, as Horace asks?
pairs.derivation: The potter's image for a work that changes shape in the making, a proverbial line. Anchored to the amphora + the wheel; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Aemilium circa ludum faber imus et unguis exprimet et mollis imitabitur aere capillos,
pairs.question: Quem ludum gladiatorium Romae Horatius nominat, circa quem ille faber infimus opera fingebat?
pairs.question_en: Which gladiatorial school at Rome does Horace name, near which that lowest craftsman worked?
pairs.derivation: The ludus Aemilius, a landmark of Rome, with the bronze-workers' shops around it. Anchored to the named school; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ego cur, adquirere pauca si possum, inuideor, cum lingua Catonis et Enni sermonem patrium ditauerit et noua rerum nomina protulerit?
pairs.question: Quorum duorum virorum lingua sermonem patrium ditavisse et nova rerum nomina protulisse Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: By which two men's speech does Horace say the native tongue was enriched and new names for things brought forth?
pairs.derivation: Cato and Ennius as the enrichers of the Latin language, a standing claim of Roman literary history. Anchored to the two names; both stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Res gestae regumque ducumque et tristia bella quo scribi possent numero, monstrauit Homerus.
pairs.question: Quis poeta monstravit quo numero res gestae regum ducumque et tristia bella scribi possent?
pairs.question_en: Which poet showed in what measure the deeds of kings and captains and grim wars could be written?
pairs.derivation: Homer as the founder of the epic metre, in Horace's history of the genres. Anchored to the subject-matter of epic; one-name answer stated verbatim. Translatable fact about metre (the hexameter and its proper matter).

pairs.source_text: Versibus impariter iunctis querimonia primum, post etiam inclusa est uoti sententia compos;
pairs.question: Quae materia primum versibus impariter iunctis, id est elegis, inclusa est, ut Horatius docet?
pairs.question_en: What matter was first enclosed in unequally paired verses, that is, in elegiacs, as Horace teaches?
pairs.derivation: The elegiac couplet's first use for lament and afterwards for the fulfilled vow. Anchored to the couplet; one-word answer stated verbatim. A fact about a metre's proper matter, and so translatable.

pairs.source_text: quis tamen exiguos elegos emiserit auctor, grammatici certant et adhuc sub iudice lis est.
pairs.question: De cuius generis carminis auctore grammatici certare et litem adhuc sub iudice esse Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: About the author of which kind of poem does Horace say the grammarians contend, the case still before the judge?
pairs.derivation: The disputed inventor of elegy, and the proverbial tag adhuc sub iudice lis est. Anchored to the grammarians' quarrel; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Archilochum proprio rabies armauit iambo;
pairs.question: Quo metro rabies Archilochum armavit, ut Horatius in Arte Poetica scribit?
pairs.question_en: With what metre did rage arm Archilochus, as Horace writes in the Ars Poetica?
pairs.derivation: Archilochus as inventor and master of the iambus. Anchored by name; one-word answer stated verbatim. A fact about metre that names the metre, hence translatable.

pairs.source_text: hunc socci cepere pedem grandesque coturni, alternis aptum sermonibus et popularis uincentem strepitus et natum rebus agendis.
pairs.question: Quem pedem tam socci quam grandes coturni ceperunt, sermonibus alternis aptum?
pairs.question_en: Which foot did both the comic slipper and the high tragic buskin take over, as suited to alternating dialogue?
pairs.derivation: The iambus as the metre of drama, comic and tragic alike. Anchored to soccus and cothurnus; one-word answer supported verbatim (hunc... pedem, the iambus of the line before). Translatable.

pairs.source_text: Musa dedit fidibus diuos puerosque deorum et pugilem uictorem et equom certamine primum et iuuenum curas et libera uina referre.
pairs.question: Cui carminis generi Musa dedit divos, pugilem victorem, equum certamine primum, iuvenum curas vinaque referre?
pairs.question_en: To which kind of poetry did the Muse grant the telling of gods, victorious boxers, winning horses, young men's loves and wine?
pairs.derivation: The proper matter of lyric in Horace's division of the genres. Anchored to the listed subjects; short answer stated verbatim (fidibus).

pairs.source_text: indignatur item priuatis ac prope socco dignis carminibus narrari cena Thyestae.
pairs.question: Cuius viri cena exemplum rei tragicae apud Horatium est, quae humili sermone narrari non vult?
pairs.question_en: Whose dinner is Horace's example of tragic matter that refuses to be told in humble style?
pairs.derivation: The banquet of Thyestes, the standing type of tragic horror. Anchored to tragic decorum; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Interdum tamen et uocem comoedia tollit, iratusque Chremes tumido delitigat ore;
pairs.question: Quae persona comica apud Horatium irata tumido ore rixatur?
pairs.question_en: Which comic character, in Horace, rails in anger with swollen speech?
pairs.derivation: Chremes, the stock angry old man of Greek and Roman comedy. Anchored to comedy raising its voice; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: et tragicus plerumque dolet sermone pedestri Telephus et Peleus, cum pauper et exul uterque proicit ampullas et sesquipedalia uerba,
pairs.question: Quos duos heroas tragicos Horatius nominat, qui pauperes et exules ampullas proiciunt?
pairs.question_en: Which two tragic heroes does Horace name as poor exiles who throw away their bombast?
pairs.derivation: Telephus and Peleus, the canonical beggared heroes of the tragic stage. Anchored to tragic style; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Honoratum si forte reponis Achillem, impiger, iracundus, inexorabilis, acer iura neget sibi nata, nihil non arroget armis.
pairs.question: Qualem Achillem in scaenam reponi Horatius iubet?
pairs.question_en: What sort of Achilles does Horace require, if you bring him back on stage?
