pairs.derivation: The canonical characterisation of Achilles, the model of consistent portrayal. Anchored to Achilles; the four epithets stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sit Medea ferox inuictaque, flebilis Ino, perfidus Ixion, Io uaga, tristis Orestes.
pairs.question: Qualem Medeam in scaena esse Horatius iubet?
pairs.question_en: What sort of Medea does Horace require on stage?
pairs.derivation: Medea's canonical attributes in the list of stage characters. Anchored to Medea; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sit Medea ferox inuictaque, flebilis Ino, perfidus Ixion, Io uaga, tristis Orestes.
pairs.question: Quo epitheto Ixiona Horatius in Arte Poetica notat?
pairs.question_en: By what epithet does Horace mark Ixion in the Ars Poetica?
pairs.derivation: Ixion the treacherous, whose betrayal of his father-in-law and of Jupiter is the canonical story. Anchored to the list of stage characters; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid dignum tanto feret hic promissor hiatu? Parturient montes, nascetur ridiculus mus.
pairs.question: Quid nascetur, cum montes parturient, ut in Arte Poetica legitur?
pairs.question_en: What will be born when the mountains go into labour, as the Ars Poetica has it?
pairs.derivation: One of the most quoted lines in Latin, Horace's mock of the grandiose opening. Anchored to the line's first half; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: "Dic mihi, Musa, uirum, captae post tempora Troiae qui mores hominum multorum uidit et urbes".
pairs.question: Cuius carminis Graeci principium Horatius Latine reddit verbis 'dic mihi, Musa, virum'?
pairs.question_en: Which Greek poem's opening does Horace render into Latin with the words 'tell me, Muse, of the man'?
pairs.derivation: Horace's Latin version of the first lines of the Odyssey, held up as the model of a modest beginning. Anchored to the quoted opening; one-name answer supported by the content of the quotation.

pairs.source_text: semper ad euentum festinat et in medias res non secus ac notas auditorem rapit,
pairs.question: Quo modo Homerum auditorem rapere Horatius dicit, cum semper ad eventum festinet?
pairs.question_en: How does Horace say Homer sweeps his hearer along, always hastening to the outcome?
pairs.derivation: The phrase in medias res, coined here and used ever since of narrative technique. Anchored to Homer's practice; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: si plosoris eges aulaea manentis et usque sessuri donec cantor. "Vos plaudite" dicat.
pairs.question: Quibus verbis cantor in fine fabulae Romanae spectatores plaudere iubebat?
pairs.question_en: With what words did the cantor call for applause at the end of a Roman play?
pairs.derivation: The formula that closed Roman comedies (cf. the endings of Plautus and Terence). Anchored to the end of the play + the cantor; the formula quoted verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ne pueros coram populo Medea trucidet, aut humana palam coquat exta nefarius Atreus,
pairs.question: Quid Medeam coram populo in scaena facere Horatius vetat?
pairs.question_en: What does Horace forbid Medea to do on stage in front of the audience?
pairs.derivation: The rule that atrocities happen offstage, with Medea's child-murder as the example. Anchored to Medea + the stage; short answer stated verbatim. Dramatic convention, translatable.

pairs.source_text: aut humana palam coquat exta nefarius Atreus, aut in auem Procne uertatur, Cadmus in anguem.
pairs.question: Quis rex humana exta coquit, quod in scaena palam fieri Horatius vetat?
pairs.question_en: Which king cooks human flesh, a thing Horace forbids to be done openly on stage?
pairs.derivation: Atreus' cannibal banquet, the canonical horror of tragedy. Anchored to the stage prohibition; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: aut in auem Procne uertatur, Cadmus in anguem.
pairs.question: In quam bestiam Procne mutata est, ut Horatius commemorat?
pairs.question_en: Into what creature was Procne changed, as Horace recalls?
pairs.derivation: Procne's metamorphosis into a bird, canonical Greek myth. Anchored by name; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: aut in auem Procne uertatur, Cadmus in anguem.
pairs.question: In quam bestiam Cadmus mutatus est, ut Horatius commemorat?
pairs.question_en: Into what creature was Cadmus changed, as Horace recalls?
pairs.derivation: Cadmus turned into a serpent, the close of the Theban founder's story. Anchored by name; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Neue minor neu sit quinto productior actu fabula, quae posci uolt et spectanda reponi;
pairs.question: Quot actus fabulam habere oportere Horatius in Arte Poetica praecipit?
pairs.question_en: How many acts does Horace prescribe for a play in the Ars Poetica?
pairs.derivation: The five-act rule, the most influential single prescription of ancient dramatic theory. Anchored to the play that wants to be revived; a number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nec deus intersit, nisi dignus uindice nodus inciderit;
pairs.question: Quando deum in scaenam intervenire Horatius permittit?
pairs.question_en: When does Horace allow a god to intervene on stage?
pairs.answer_en: Only when a knot has arisen that deserves such a deliverer.
pairs.derivation: The rule of the deus ex machina. Anchored to the stage god; short answer stated verbatim. Dramatic convention, translatable.

pairs.source_text: nec quarta loqui persona laboret.
pairs.question: Quot personae in scaena loqui debent, ut Horatius praecipit?
pairs.answer: Tres; quarta enim loqui non debet.
pairs.question_en: How many characters should speak on stage, by Horace's rule?
pairs.answer_en: Three; a fourth should not try to speak.
pairs.derivation: The three-actor rule of ancient drama, stated by Horace as the ban on a fourth speaking part. Anchored to the stage; short answer stated verbatim in substance (nec quarta loqui persona laboret).

pairs.source_text: Actoris partis chorus officiumque uirile defendat, neu quid medios intercinat actus, quod non proposito conducat et haereat apte.
pairs.question: Quas partes chorum in fabula sustinere Horatius iubet?
pairs.question_en: What part does Horace require the chorus to sustain in a play?
pairs.answer_en: An actor's part and a man's duty.
pairs.derivation: The function of the dramatic chorus, and the ban on irrelevant interludes between acts. Anchored to the chorus; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tibia non, ut nunc, orichalco uincta tubaeque aemula, sed tenuis simplexque foramine pauco adspirare et adesse choris erat utilis
pairs.question: Qualis olim tibia fuit, antequam orichalco vinciretur et tubae aemula fieret, ut Horatius describit?
pairs.question_en: What was the pipe like in the old days, before it was bound with brass and rivalled the trumpet, as Horace describes it?
pairs.answer_en: Thin and simple, with few holes.
pairs.derivation: The early Roman tibia, slender and few-holed, before theatrical music grew grand. Anchored to the old theatre; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Carmine qui tragico uilem certauit ob hircum, mox etiam agrestis Satyros nudauit et asper incolumi grauitate iocum temptauit
pairs.question: Quod vile praemium olim in tragici carminis certamine petebatur, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: What cheap prize was once competed for in the contest of tragic song, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: The goat-prize of the tragic contest, the standard ancient explanation of the name 'tragedy'. Anchored to the contest; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: inlecebris erat et grata nouitate morandus spectator functusque sacris et potus et exlex.
pairs.question: Quales spectatores novitate Satyrorum morandi erant, ut Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: What sort of spectators had to be held by the novelty of the satyr-play, as Horace says?
pairs.answer_en: Those who had finished the rites, drunk and lawless.
pairs.derivation: The satyr play placed after the tragedies to hold an audience fresh from the sacrifices and the wine. Anchored to the satyr play; short answer stated verbatim. Festival-theatre custom.

pairs.source_text: ut nihil intersit Dauusne loquatur et audax Pythias, emuncto lucrata Simone talentum, an custos famulusque dei Silenus alumni.
pairs.question: Quis in fabulis Satyricis custos et famulus dei alumni inducitur?
pairs.question_en: Who is brought on in satyr plays as guardian and servant of the god he nursed?
pairs.derivation: Silenus, tutor of the young Bacchus and standing character of the satyr play. Anchored to the satyr drama; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nec sic enitar tragico diferre colori ut nihil intersit Dauusne loquatur et audax Pythias, emuncto lucrata Simone talentum,
pairs.question: Quo nomine servus comicus apud Horatium exempli causa appellatur?
pairs.question_en: By what name is the comic slave called in Horace's example?
pairs.derivation: Davus, the canonical name of the slave in Roman comedy (as in Terence). Anchored to comic characters; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: offenduntur enim quibus est equos et pater et res, nec, siquid fricti ciceris probat et nucis emptor, aequis accipiunt animis donantue corona.
pairs.question: Quas res humiliores spectatores in ludis emere solebant, ut Horatius indicat?
pairs.question_en: What did the humbler spectators buy at the shows, as Horace indicates?
pairs.derivation: The cheap snacks of the Roman theatre crowd, set against the knights with horse, father and property. Anchored to the audience; both items stated verbatim. Food-and-spectacle culture.

pairs.source_text: Syllaba longa breui subiecta uocatur iambus, pes citus; unde etiam trimetris adcrescere iussit nomen iambeis, cum senos redderet ictus,
pairs.question: Quot ictus versus iambicus trimeter reddit, ut Horatius docet?
pairs.question_en: How many beats does the iambic trimeter render, as Horace teaches?
pairs.derivation: The iambic trimeter is so called though it yields six beats (three double feet). A fact about metre statable in any language, hence on the translatable track. Anchored to the named verse; a number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vos exemplaria Graeca nocturna uersate manu, uersate diurna.
pairs.question: Quae exemplaria Horatius Pisones nocturna diurnaque manu versare iubet?
pairs.question_en: Which models does Horace tell the Pisos to thumb by night and by day?
pairs.derivation: The programmatic command of the Ars Poetica, endlessly quoted. Anchored to Horace + the Pisos; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: At uestri proaui Plautinos et numeros et laudauere sales, nimium patienter utrumque, ne dicam stulte, mirati,
pairs.question: Cuius poetae numeros et sales proavi Pisonum nimium patienter laudaverunt, ut Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: Whose measures and whose jests did the Pisos' forefathers praise far too tolerantly, as Horace says?
pairs.derivation: Horace's verdict on Plautus and on the old Romans' taste. Anchored to the ancestors' praise; one-name answer stated verbatim. Literary history, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Ignotum tragicae genus inuenisse Camenae dicitur et plaustris uexisse poemata Thespis
pairs.question: Quis tragoediae genus ignotum invenisse et plaustris poemata vexisse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented the unknown kind of tragic song and carried his poems about on wagons?
pairs.derivation: Thespis, inventor of tragedy and the wagon-stage, in the standard ancient account. Anchored to the invention of tragedy; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: dicitur et plaustris uexisse poemata Thespis quae canerent agerentque peruncti faecibus ora.
pairs.question: Qua re histriones apud Thespin ora perunguebant, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: With what did Thespis' performers smear their faces, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: The lees-smeared faces of the earliest tragic performers, before the mask. Anchored to Thespis; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Post hunc personae pallaeque repertor honestae Aeschylus et modicis instrauit pulpita tignis
pairs.question: Quis personae pallaeque honestae repertor fuisse dicitur, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have been the inventor of the mask and the noble robe, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: Aeschylus credited with the tragic mask, the stately costume and the raised stage. Anchored to the invention; one-name answer stated verbatim. Theatre history, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Aeschylus et modicis instrauit pulpita tignis et docuit magnumque loqui nitique coturno.
pairs.question: Quo calceamento niti histriones Aeschylus docuit?
pairs.question_en: In what footwear did Aeschylus teach actors to stride?
pairs.derivation: The cothurnus as the mark of tragedy, taught by Aeschylus (against the comic soccus). Anchored to Aeschylus; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Successit uetus his comoedia, non sine multa laude; sed in uitium libertas excidit et uim dignam lege regi; lex est accepta chorusque turpiter obticuit sublato iure nocendi.
pairs.question: Quid Veteri Comoediae accidit, lege accepta, ut Horatius narrat?
pairs.question_en: What happened to Old Comedy when the law was passed, as Horace tells it?
pairs.derivation: The silencing of the Old Comic chorus once a law curbed its licence to injure. Anchored to Old Comedy + the law; short answer stated verbatim. Dramatic history, translatable.

pairs.source_text: nec minimum meruere decus uestigia Graeca ausi deserere et celebrare domestica facta, uel qui praetextas uel qui docuere togatas.
pairs.question: Quibus duobus fabularum generibus poetae Romani domestica facta celebraverunt, ut Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: By which two kinds of play did Roman poets celebrate home-grown deeds, as Horace says?
pairs.derivation: The two native Roman dramatic genres: the praetexta (historical) and the togata (Roman-dress comedy). Anchored to the Roman poets; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vos, o Pompilius sanguis, carmen reprehendite quod non multa dies et multa litura coercuit atque praesectum deciens non castigauit ad unguem.
pairs.question: Quotiens ad unguem castigatum esse carmen Horatius postulat?
pairs.question_en: How many times over does Horace require a poem to have been trimmed to the fingernail?
pairs.derivation: The demand for repeated correction, source of the phrase ad unguem. Anchored to the Pisos + the poem; a number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ingenium misera quia fortunatius arte credit et excludit sanos Helicone poetas Democritus, bona pars non unguis ponere curat, non barbam, secreta petit loca, balnea uitat;
pairs.question: Quis philosophus sanos poetas Helicone excludere creditur, ingenium arti praeferens?
pairs.question_en: Which philosopher is believed to shut sane poets out of Helicon, preferring genius to art?
pairs.derivation: Democritus' doctrine of poetic madness, the source of the unkempt poet's pose. Anchored to Helicon + the doctrine; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nanciscetur enim pretium nomenque poetae, si tribus Anticyris caput insanabile nunquam tonsori Licino commiserit.
pairs.question: Quot Anticyrae caput poetae furentis sanare non possint, ut Horatius iocatur?
pairs.question_en: How many Anticyras, in Horace's joke, could not cure the mad poet's head?
pairs.derivation: Anticyra, the town of hellebore, is the proverbial cure for madness; three of them would not serve. Anchored to the mad poet; a number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Scribendi recte sapere est et principium et fons.
pairs.question: Quam rem Horatius scribendi recte et principium et fontem esse dicit?
pairs.question_en: What does Horace call both the beginning and the fountainhead of writing well?
pairs.derivation: A much-quoted Horatian tag; its checkable point is what stands in the predicate. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Romani pueri longis rationibus assem discunt in partis centum diducere.
pairs.question: In quot partes Romani pueri assem diducere discebant, ut Horatius scribit?
pairs.question_en: Into how many parts did Roman boys learn to divide the as, as Horace writes?
pairs.derivation: The Roman schoolroom's arithmetic of fractions of the as. Anchored to Roman boys + the as; a number stated verbatim. Education and money, translatable.

pairs.source_text: filius Albini: si de quincunce remota est uncia, quid superat?. . . Poteras dixisse. — Triens. — Eu!
pairs.question: Quid superat, si de quincunce uncia remota est, ut in ludo Romano discebatur?
pairs.question_en: What is left if an ounce is taken from a quincunx, as was learned in the Roman schoolroom?
pairs.derivation: The fractions of the as: quincunx (5/12) less uncia (1/12) leaves triens (4/12). Anchored to the school exercise; the answer stated verbatim. Money-reckoning every Roman carried.

pairs.source_text: Rem poteris seruare tuam. Redit uncia, quid fit? "Semis".
pairs.question: Quid fit, si ad quincuncem uncia redit, ut in ludo Romano respondebatur?
pairs.question_en: What do you get if the ounce is added back to the quincunx, as the Roman schoolroom answered?
pairs.derivation: The second half of the schoolroom sum: quincunx (5/12) plus uncia (1/12) makes semis (6/12). Anchored to the same exercise; the answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Aut prodesse uolunt aut delectare poetae aut simul et iucunda et idonea dicere uitae.
pairs.question: Quid poetas velle Horatius in Arte Poetica dicit?
pairs.question_en: What does Horace say poets want to do, in the Ars Poetica?
pairs.answer_en: Either to profit or to please.
pairs.derivation: The formula that governed later criticism (prodesse et delectare). Anchored to the poets; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ficta uoluptatis causa sint proxima ueris, ne quodcumque uolet poscat sibi fabula credi, neu pransae Lamiae uiuum puerum extrahat aluo.
pairs.question: Cuius monstri alvo puer vivus extrahi non debet, ut Horatius vetat?
pairs.question_en: From what monster's belly must a living boy not be dragged, in Horace's prohibition?
pairs.derivation: Lamia, the child-devouring bogey of ancient nursery tale. Anchored to the stage prohibition; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Centuriae seniorum agitant expertia frugis, celsi praetereunt austera poemata Ramnes.
pairs.question: Quo nomine Horatius iuvenes equites appellat, qui austera poemata praetereunt?
pairs.question_en: By what name does Horace call the young knights who pass over austere poems?
pairs.derivation: Ramnes, one of the three original centuries of Roman knights, used for the young nobility of the theatre audience. Anchored to the audience; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Omne tulit punctum qui miscuit utile dulci, lectorem delectando pariterque monendo;
pairs.question: Quis omne punctum tulit, ut in Arte Poetica legitur?
pairs.question_en: Who has won every vote, as the Ars Poetica has it?
pairs.answer_en: He who has mixed the useful with the sweet.
pairs.derivation: One of the most quoted lines of the Ars Poetica; the image is of the ballot-marks (puncta). Anchored to the line's opening; short answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: et idem indignor quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus; uerum operi longo fas est obrepere somnum.
pairs.question: Quem poetam Horatius interdum dormitare dicit, cum de operis longi maculis loquitur?
pairs.question_en: Which poet does Horace say sometimes nods, when he speaks of the blemishes of a long work?
pairs.derivation: Quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus, proverbial ever since. Anchored to the quoted line; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vt pictura poesis; erit quae, si propius stes, te capiat magis, et quaedam, si longius abstes;
pairs.question: Cui arti Horatius poesin in Arte Poetica comparat?
pairs.question_en: To which art does Horace compare poetry in the Ars Poetica?
pairs.derivation: Ut pictura poesis, the tag that founded a whole tradition of criticism. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: sed tamen in pretio est; mediocribus esse poetis non homines, non di, non concessere columnae.
pairs.question: Qui tres poetis mediocribus esse non concesserunt, ut Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: Which three have refused poets leave to be middling, as Horace says?
pairs.answer_en: Men, gods and the booksellers' pillars.
pairs.derivation: The famous denial of middling poetry, with the columnae (the pillars where books were advertised) as the third judge. Anchored to poets; the three stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vt gratas inter mensas symphonia discors et crassum unguentum et Sardo cum melle papauer offendunt,
pairs.question: Cuius insulae mel amarum inter cenae offensiones Horatius numerat?
pairs.question_en: Which island's bitter honey does Horace count among the offences of a dinner?
pairs.derivation: Sardinian honey, proverbially bitter, served with poppy-seed. Anchored to the dinner table; the item stated verbatim. Food knowledge, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Ludere qui nescit, campestribus abstinet armis, indoctusque pilae disciue trochiue quiescit, ne spissae risum tollant impune coronae;
pairs.question: Quibus tribus ludis Romani in Campo exercebantur, quos Horatius nominat?
pairs.question_en: In which three games did Romans exercise on the Campus, as Horace names them?
pairs.derivation: The standard exercises of the Campus Martius. Anchored to the Campus; the three stated verbatim. Leisure custom, translatable.

pairs.source_text: Tu nihil inuita dices faciesue Minerua; id tibi iudicium est, ea mens.
pairs.question: Qua dea invita nihil dicendum aut faciendum esse Horatius monet?
pairs.question_en: Against which goddess's will does Horace warn one to say or do nothing?
pairs.derivation: The proverb invita Minerva, of working against one's natural gift. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Siquid tamen olim scripseris, in Maeci descendat iudicis auris et patris et nostras, nonumque prematur in annum membranis intus positis;
pairs.question: In quotum annum carmen premi Horatius iubet antequam edatur?
pairs.question_en: Until which year does Horace order a poem to be kept back before publication?
pairs.derivation: Nonum prematur in annum, the most quoted counsel of literary patience. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; a number stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: delere licebit quod non edideris; nescit uox missa reuerti.
pairs.question: Quid, semel emissum, reverti nescire Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: What, once let go, does Horace say cannot come back?
pairs.derivation: Nescit uox missa reuerti, a proverbial line on the irrevocability of publication. Anchored to the Ars Poetica; one-word answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Siluestris homines sacer interpresque deorum caedibus et uictu foedo deterruit Orpheus, dictus ob hoc lenire tigris rabidosque leones;
pairs.question: Quis vates tigris rabidosque leones lenisse dicitur, qui homines silvestris a caedibus deterruit?
pairs.question_en: Which bard is said to have soothed tigers and raging lions, having turned wild men from slaughter?
pairs.derivation: Orpheus as civiliser and tamer of beasts, canonical myth. Anchored by the deeds; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: dictus et Amphion, Thebanae conditor urbis, saxa mouere sono testudinis et prece blanda ducere quo uellet.
pairs.question: Quis Thebanae urbis conditor saxa sono testudinis movisse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Which founder of the city of Thebes is said to have moved stones by the sound of his lyre?
pairs.derivation: Amphion building Thebes with his lyre, canonical myth. Anchored to Thebes; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Post hos insignis Homerus Tyrtaeusque mares animos in Martia bella uersibus exacuit,
pairs.question: Quos duos poetas Horatius dicit versibus mares animos in Martia bella exacuisse?
pairs.question_en: Which two poets does Horace say sharpened manly spirits for the wars of Mars with their verses?
pairs.derivation: Homer and Tyrtaeus as the martial poets in Horace's account of poetry's civic uses. Anchored to the deed; both names stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: abstinuit uenere et uino; qui Pythia cantat tibicen, didicit prius extimuitque magistrum.
pairs.question: In quibus certaminibus Graecis canit ille tibicen, quem Horatius exemplum laboris ponit?
pairs.question_en: At which Greek games does the piper play whom Horace holds up as an example of training?
pairs.derivation: The Pythian games at Delphi, where the pipers competed. Anchored to the piper; the games named verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vt qui conducti plorant in funere dicunt et faciunt prope plura dolentibus ex animo, sic derisor uero plus laudatore mouetur.
pairs.question: Qui homines in funere Romano plura quam ex animo dolentes faciunt, ut Horatius dicit?
pairs.question_en: Who, at a Roman funeral, weep and do almost more than those who truly grieve, as Horace says?
pairs.derivation: The hired mourners of the Roman funeral, whose grief outdoes the family's. Anchored to the funeral; one-word answer stated verbatim. Funerary custom.

pairs.source_text: Quintilio siquid recitares: "Corrige, sodes, hoc" aiebat "et hoc"; melius te posse negares, bis terque expertum frustra; delere iubebat
pairs.question: Quis criticus, cum quid ei recitaretur, 'corrige, sodes, hoc et hoc' dicere solebat, ut Horatius narrat?
pairs.question_en: Which critic used to say 'correct this, please, and this' when something was recited to him, as Horace tells it?
pairs.derivation: Quintilius Varus, the honest critic of the Augustan circle (mourned in Odes 1.24). Anchored to the recitation; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: arguet ambigue dictum, mutanda notabit, fiet Aristarchus, nec dicet: "Cur ego amicum offendam in nugis?"
pairs.question: Cuius grammatici Graeci nomen Horatius pro severo carminum iudice ponit?
pairs.question_en: Which Greek scholar's name does Horace use for the severe judge of poems?
pairs.derivation: Aristarchus of Samothrace, the Homeric critic, as the byword for rigorous textual judgement. Anchored to the honest critic; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vt mala quem scabies aut morbus regius urget aut fanaticus error et iracunda Diana, uesanum tetigisse timent fugiuntque poetam,
pairs.question: Cuius deae ira apud Horatium inter mentis morbos numeratur?
pairs.question_en: Which goddess's anger does Horace count among the diseases of the mind?
pairs.derivation: The wrath of Diana as a cause of madness, listed with jaundice (morbus regius) and fanatical frenzy. Anchored to the list of afflictions; one-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Siculique poetae narrabo interitum. Deus inmortalis haberi dum cupit Empedocles, ardentem frigidus Aetnam insiluit.
pairs.question: In quem montem Empedocles insiluisse dicitur, deus immortalis haberi cupiens?
pairs.question_en: Into which mountain is Empedocles said to have leapt, wishing to be held an immortal god?
pairs.derivation: The death of Empedocles in the crater of Etna, one of the best-known stories of ancient philosophy. Anchored to Empedocles; one place-name answer stated verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec satis apparet cur uersus factitet, utrum minxerit in patrios cineres, an triste bidental mouerit incestus;
pairs.question: Quam rem sacram, fulmine tactam, poeta furens movisse fingitur apud Horatium?
pairs.question_en: What consecrated thing, struck by lightning, is the mad poet imagined to have disturbed, in Horace?
pairs.derivation: The bidental, the spot struck by lightning and fenced off as sacred, which it was sacrilege to disturb. Anchored to the poet's supposed impiety; the term stated verbatim. Roman religious practice.
